claim: HIV-1 contains nine genes encoded within a genome of approximately 10,000 nucleotides.
source: HIV-1 contains nine genes encoded within a relatively short genome of 10,000 nucleotides (Frankel and Young, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frankel and Young, 1998

claim: Eight of the nine HIV-1 genes overlap with another gene on the DNA level.
source: Eight of these nine genes overlap with another on the DNA level and consequently encode protein products in different reading frames.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the manuscript

claim: HIV-1 Env overlaps with Vpu, Rev, and Tat genes.
source: HIV-1 Env overlaps with Vpu, Rev, and Tat, and some parts of Env overlap with both Rev and Tat.
evidence: Stated as established fact in the manuscript

claim: Many immune epitopes targeting canonical and non-canonical overlapping ORFs have been identified in SARS-CoV-2 patients.
source: the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has demonstrated the importance of identifying and studying overlapping reading frames, as many immune epitopes targeting canonical and non-canonical overlapping ORFs (open reading frames) have been identified in patients (Nelson et al., 2020; Weingarten-Gabbay et al., 2020;; Finkel et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nelson et al., 2020; Weingarten-Gabbay et al., 2020; Finkel et al., 2021

claim: In HIV-1 tat and rev genes, critical functional residues do not overlap with one another.
source: We previously showed that, in the case of the essential regulatory genes tat and rev, HIV-1 dedicates the nucleotide sequence to one protein or the other so that critical functional residues do not overlap with one another (Fernandes et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by Fernandes et al., 2016

claim: For tat and rev, functional motifs of one protein can be encoded in regions that overlap with disordered linkers in the other.
source: For tat and rev, this arrangement is possible because both proteins consist of functional motifs spaced by disordered linkers, and thus functional motifs of one protein can be encoded in regions that overlap with disordered linkers in the other.
evidence: Logical explanation based on structural properties of the proteins

claim: The vast majority of overlapped proteins are predicted to be disordered.
source: Although the vast majority of overlapped proteins are predicted to be disordered (Rancurel et al., 2009) and thus have the potential for this arrangement, it is possible that some overlapped regions have more stringent structure and function requirements.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rancurel et al., 2009

claim: HIV-1 contains an overlapping region between Rev and Env genes in which both protein segments are structured and functionally important.
source: Indeed, HIV-1 contains an intriguing overlapping region, between the Rev and Env genes (Figure 1A), in which both protein segments are structured and functionally important.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Rev is required for the nuclear export of partially spliced and un-spliced viral RNAs.
source: Rev is required for the nuclear export of partially spliced and un-spliced viral RNAs that encode necessary late stage viral proteins as well as the genomic RNA for encapsidation (Malim and Cullen, 1991; Pollard and Malim, 1998; Rausch and Le Grice, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Malim and Cullen, 1991; Pollard and Malim, 1998; Rausch and Le Grice, 2015

claim: Rev contains a quasi-helical nuclear export sequence (NES) that binds to the NES-binding groove of Crm1.
source: Notably, Rev contains a quasi-helical nuclear export sequence (NES), that binds to the NES-binding groove of the host nuclear export factor Crm1 (Fornerod et al., 1997; Booth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fornerod et al., 1997; Booth et al., 2014

claim: Env is expressed as a polyprotein composed of gp120 surface and gp41 transmembrane proteins.
source: Env is expressed as a polyprotein, composed of the gp120 surface and gp41 transmembrane proteins, which forms a trimeric viral envelope that mediates viral particle binding to cell entry receptors (Checkley et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Checkley et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2017

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of gp41 is highly variable in size.
source: The cytoplasmic tail of gp41 is the most C-terminal portion of Env and is highly variable in size (Tedbury and Freed, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tedbury and Freed, 2015

claim: Lentiviruses such as HIV-1 have an extended cytoplasmic tail containing the Kennedy epitope (KE) followed by three lentiviral lytic peptide motifs (LLP-1, LLP-2, and LLP-3).
source: In contrast to other retroviruses, lentiviruses such as HIV-1 have an extended cytoplasmic tail containing the Kennedy epitope (KE) followed by three membrane associated lentiviral lytic peptide motifs (LLP-1, LLP-2, and LLP-3) (Steckbeck et al., 2013; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steckbeck et al., 2013 and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: HIV-1 LLP-1 and LLP-2 contain highly conserved arginine and lysine residues involved in cation-π interactions.
source: HIV-1 LLP-1, and LLP-2 contain highly conserved arginine and lysine residues that are involved in cation-π interactions and have been suggested to stabilize the cytoplasmic tail α-helical structure (Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy et al., 2017

claim: LLPs are amphipathic α helices that embed in virus membranes.
source: LLPs are amphipathic α helices that embed in the virus membranes (Kalia et al., 2003; Steckbeck et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalia et al., 2003; Steckbeck et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2017

claim: LLP-2 may be transiently exposed on the virus surface to interact with the gp41 core and regulate virus-cell membrane fusion.
source: LLP-2 may be transiently exposed on the virus surface to interact with the gp41 core and regulate virus-cell membrane fusion (Lu et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2017; Piai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2017; Piai et al., 2020

claim: LLP-2 forms two amphipathic helices that wrap around the transmembrane domain of Env, forming a 'baseplate' that supports the transmembrane domain and the rest of the Env trimer.
source: A recent nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy study revealed that LLP-2 forms two amphipathic helices that wrap around the transmembrane domain of Env, arranging a 'baseplate' that supports the transmembrane domain and the rest of the Env trimer (Piai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piai et al., 2020

claim: The C-terminal tail of Env makes critical contacts with the matrix protein to facilitate Env incorporation into virions.
source: Additional evidence suggests that the C-terminal tail makes critical contacts with the matrix protein (Alfadhli et al., 2019) to facilitate Env incorporation into virions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Alfadhli et al., 2019

claim: The Rev NES (residues 75–83) and a portion of the Env LLP-2 are encoded by the same nucleotides in the viral genome, with Env encoded in the +1 reading frame relative to Rev.
source: The Rev NES and a portion of the Env LLP-2 are encoded by the same nucleotides in the viral genome, with Env encoded in the +1 reading frame relative to Rev (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: The Rev NES binds to Crm1 using several critical hydrophobic residues and non-canonical prolines that change the helical register.
source: The Rev NES (residues 75–83) binds to Crm1 using several critical hydrophobic residues and non-canonical prolines that change the helical register and position hydrophobic side chains on one face of the helix to fit within the NES recognition groove (Dong et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2009; Güttler et al., 2010 and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: The Env LLP-2 forms an amphipathic helix of about 33 amino acids long spanning residues 767–788 of Env.
source: The Env LLP-2 forms an amphipathic helix of about 33 amino acids long (Eisenberg and Wesson, 1990; Kalia et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2017) that spans residues 767–788 of Env (242–274 of gp41) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eisenberg and Wesson, 1990; Kalia et al., 2003; Murphy et al., 2017 and illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: Nine of the LLP-2 residues (767–776) overlap with the quasi-helical Rev NES.
source: Nine of the LLP-2 residues (767–776) overlap with the quasi-helical Rev NES (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: Mutating charged residues within LLP-2 or hydrophobic residues in the Rev NES negatively impacts viral replication.
source: Mutating charged residues within LLP-2 or hydrophobic residues in the Rev NES negatively impacts viral replication (Kalia et al., 2003; Newman et al., 2007; Güttler et al., 2010; Fernandes et al., 2016), prompting us to examine in detail the selective forces that guide the evolution of this overlapping region.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalia et al., 2003; Newman et al., 2007; Güttler et al., 2010; Fernandes et al., 2016

claim: The site containing H769 in Env and P76 in Rev is relatively well conserved in both proteins.
source: Notably, the one site that contributes to both functional surfaces (H769 in Env and P76 in Rev) is relatively well conserved in both proteins whereas the one site that contributes to neither interface (L755 in Env and T82 in Rev) is weakly conserved (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on entropy analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: The site containing L755 in Env and T82 in Rev is weakly conserved.
source: Notably, the one site that contributes to both functional surfaces (H769 in Env and P76 in Rev) is relatively well conserved in both proteins whereas the one site that contributes to neither interface (L755 in Env and T82 in Rev) is weakly conserved (Figure 2A).
evidence: Based on entropy analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Two known essential Crm1-binding residues (L78 and L83) displayed low conservation (high entropy) in the Rev reading frame, but chemically conservative isoleucine substitutions are frequently found.
source: Unexpectedly, two known essential Crm1-binding residues (L78 and L83) displayed low conservation (high entropy) in the Rev reading frame, but the consensus sequence (Figure 2B) indicates that chemically conservative isoleucine substitutions are frequently found, thus explaining the high entropy.
evidence: Based on entropy analysis and sequence logos shown in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: Entropy analysis using a reduced amino acid alphabet in which chemically similar amino acids I/L/V are grouped produced low entropy values for all Crm1-binding residues.
source: Moreover, entropy analysis using a reduced amino acid alphabet in which the chemically similar amino acids I/L/V are grouped produced low entropy values for all Crm1-binding residues (Figure 2C).
evidence: Based on reduced alphabet entropy analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: The use of chemically conservative side chains to form critical contacts drastically increases the number of 'synonymous' codons.
source: The use of chemically conservative side chains to form critical contacts drastically increases the number of 'synonymous' codons (e.g. the six leucine codons can substitute with the three isoleucine codons with essentially equal fitness) and may reflect the kinds of interaction motifs that are most suited to evolve in constrained overlapping regions.
evidence: Logical inference from the observation of chemically conservative substitutions

claim: Three charged residues in LLP-2 were relatively strongly conserved but showed lower conservation than the Rev NES-binding residues.
source: The three charged residues (Figure 2C; green dots) in LLP-2 were relatively strongly conserved (Figure 2B) but showed lower conservation (high entropy) than the Rev NES-binding residues, suggesting that Rev may more greatly influence the selection of amino acids in the overlapping region.
evidence: Based on entropy analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2C

claim: The LLP-2 fitness landscape shows that LLP-2 is generally highly mutable but has a strong preference for a negatively charged side chain (D or E) at residue 773.
source: The LLP-2 fitness landscape shows that while LLP-2 is generally highly mutable, it has a strong preference for a negatively charged side chain (D or E) at residue 773 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The LLP-2 fitness landscape shows strong selection against the 'helix-breaker' proline at all positions.
source: The data also show strong selection against the 'helix-breaker' proline (Li et al., 1996) at all positions, further underscoring the importance of its helical structure.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data and citation to Li et al., 1996

claim: Stop codons in LLP-2 are robustly selected against, demonstrating the importance of the cytoplasmic tail in HIV-1 replication.
source: Stop codons are robustly selected against as well, demonstrating the importance of the cytoplasmic tail in HIV-1 replication.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data

claim: L771 in LLP-2 displays a strong preference against charged residues.
source: Additionally, L771, which is surrounded by two positively charged arginines, displays a strong preference against charged residues.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data

claim: The Rev NES fitness landscape shows selection for large hydrophobic side chains (ILV) at each Crm1 contacting residue.
source: The Rev NES fitness landscape is consistent with many mutational studies, showing selection for large hydrophobic side chains (ILV) at each Crm1 contacting residue.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Unlike LLP-2, there is no selection against proline in the semi-helical Rev NES, consistent with the presence of prolines in its reference sequence.
source: Unlike LLP-2, we do not observe selection against proline in the semi-helical Rev NES, consistent with the presence of prolines in its reference sequence.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data

claim: Mutation of any of the leucines (positions 75, 78, 81, and 83) or proline at position 76 in the Rev NES resulted in loss of function.
source: Mutation of any of the leucines (positions 75, 78, 81, and 83) or proline at position 76 resulted in loss of function (Figure 4A; high p24=active Rev), consistent with previous data of Crm1-binding residues (Figure 1C; Fornerod et al., 1997; Güttler et al., 2010; Booth et al., 2014; Jayaraman et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on Rev reporter assay data shown in Figure 4A and supported by citations

claim: Mutation of the NES non-binding face had limited impact on Rev function.
source: Consistent with our selection data, mutation of the NES non-binding face had limited impact on Rev function.
evidence: Based on Rev reporter assay data

claim: The D773A mutation in Env LLP-2 produced the most drastic phenotype (15% of wild-type Env).
source: The D773A mutation produced the most drastic phenotype (15% of wild-type Env), consistent with our selection data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The first arginine in LLP-2 (R770) is important for Env function.
source: Previous work noted the conservation of arginines within the LLPs (Kalia et al., 2005; Steckbeck et al., 2011) and our data confirms that the first arginine in LLP-2 (R770) is also important for Env function, in addition to D773.
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay data and supported by citations to Kalia et al., 2005; Steckbeck et al., 2011

claim: D773E, a conservative change, showed ~50% of wild-type activity in the reporter assay.
source: D773E, a conservative change predicted to maintain function based on our fitness data, showed ~50% of wild-type activity in the reporter assay, but substantially higher than the non-conservative D773A and D773N substitutions (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: D773A viruses can replicate, albeit poorly, despite very low activity in reporter assays.
source: It is interesting that D773A viruses still can replicate, albeit poorly, despite its very low activity; these results suggest that the virus can partially compensate for the loss of function, particularly when not competing with the wild-type sequence.
evidence: Based on viral replication assay data shown in Figure 5A

claim: The weakly active D773N allele is observed in ~2.6% of patient isolates.
source: The weakly active D773N allele is observed in ~2.6% of patient isolates (Figure 2B), further suggesting that the virus has alternative mechanisms to achieve the function normally performed by the negative charge at this position.
evidence: Based on patient sequence data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mutation of R770 was particularly detrimental in combination with D773.
source: We generated two double mutants with D773/R770 or D773/R772 changed to alanine (R1D→AA or R2D→AA) as well as the triple mutant (RRD→AAA) and found that mutation of R770 was particularly detrimental, in combination with D773 which is about one helical turn away (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay and viral replication data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Both double mutants (R1D→AA and R2D→AA) showed significantly decreased virus replication.
source: Both of the double mutants showed significantly decreased virus replication (Figure 5B), again suggesting loss of function can be partially compensated in the viral context for the loss of function.
evidence: Based on viral replication data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The triple mutant (RRD→AAA) was highly defective in both reporter and replication assays.
source: The triple mutant was highly defective in both reporter and replication assays indicating the importance of these charged residues.
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay and viral replication data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Western blots of R1D mutant virions indicated decreased Env protein stability.
source: Western blots of these virions indicated decreased Env protein stability for R1D.
evidence: Based on Western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The H769K mutant showed no functional phenotype in both reporter and replication assays.
source: The results show no functional phenotype for H769K mutant in both reporter and replication assays and RR→KK outcomes confirm the importance of R770 and R773 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay and viral replication data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Deep mutational scanning of Env LLP-2 reveals selection against negative charged residues (D and E) and even K for both R770 and R772.
source: While we did not examine the mutations of R770K and R773K independently out, deep mutational scanning of Env LLP-2 (Figure 3B) reveals selection against negative charged residues (D and E) and even K for both arginines, a bias is not observed in H769, suggesting that H769 is less constrained than the two arginines.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Substitution of both arginines with lysine (RR→KK) is insufficient to maintain function or replication.
source: It is interesting that substitution of both arginine with lysine is insufficient to maintain function or replication, and indeed the (RR→KK) mutant showed the most severe replication defect.
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay and viral replication data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The Env cytoplasmic tail shows enrichment for arginine and depletion for lysine when compared to the rest of Env and all other proteins in the Uniprot database.
source: Regardless of the mechanism, the data suggest that these particular residues are subject to significant evolutionary constraints. The results are also consistent with analyses of the Env cytoplasmic tail, which has shown enrichment for arginine and depletion for lysine when compared to the rest of Env and all other proteins found in the Uniprot database (Steckbeck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steckbeck et al., 2011

claim: LLP-2 forms two helices.
source: LLP-2 forms two helices (Murphy et al., 2017) and our deep mutational scanning data suggest strong selection against helix-breaking prolines, implying a structural constraint during evolution.
evidence: Supported by citation to Murphy et al., 2017 and deep mutational scanning data

claim: The 10GS variant (residues 767–776 replaced with glycines and serines) had no activity in the reporter assay and was unable to replicate.
source: To better understand the extent of this constraint, we replaced residues 767–776 with glycines and serines (10GS) to create a flexible linker. As anticipated, the 10GS variant had no activity in the reporter assay and was unable to replicate even when D773 was reintroduced (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay and viral replication data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The 10A variant (residues 767–776 replaced with alanines) was defective.
source: We next replaced residues 767–776 with alanines (10A) which are often used to form rigid helical linkers (Chen et al., 2013). This 10A variant was similarly defective (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay data shown in Figure 6B and citation to Chen et al., 2013

claim: Reintroducing important charged residues (R770 or D773 or the five-residue HRLRD segment) into the 10A variant resulted in substantial restoration of activity and rescue of virus replication, particularly when D773 was present.
source: However, in this case, reintroducing important charged residues (R770 or D773 or the five-residue HRLRD segment) resulted in substantial restoration of activity and rescue of virus replication, particularly in the cases where D773 was present (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on Env reporter assay and viral replication data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The functional surfaces of Rev NES and Env LLP-2 are positioned to minimize negative consequences of the overlap.
source: Specifically, our analysis showed that in Env, D773 has a strong preference for negative charge, R770 and R772 have an intermediate preference for arginine side chains, H769 has a weak preference for a positive charge, and L771 selects against charged side chains. When combined with the preferences of the Rev NES Crm1-binding residues (Fernandes et al., 2016), it is apparent that the functional surfaces of each domain are positioned so as to minimize negative consequences of the overlap.
evidence: Based on integration of deep mutational scanning data and previous work

claim: The non-binding face of the Rev NES largely corresponds to the charged surface of the Env LLP-2 and the hydrophobic surface of the LLP-2 corresponds to the binding residues of the Rev NES.
source: The non-binding face of the Rev NES largely corresponds to the charged surface of the Env LLP-2 and the hydrophobic surface of the LLP-2 corresponds to the binding residues of the Rev NES (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7

claim: The majority of overlaps between opposing critical residues mostly involve mutable wobble bases, with the sole exception being the Env H769/Rev P76 overlap.
source: The majority of overlaps between opposing critical residues mostly involve mutable wobble bases, with the sole exception being the Env H769/Rev P76 overlap.
evidence: Based on analysis of nucleotide sequence and functional constraints

claim: Rev appears to be the major driver of evolution at the H769/P76 overlap as mutation of P76 results in severe loss of function whereas H769 appears to play a minor, supporting role.
source: However, in this case Rev appears to be the major driver of evolution as mutation of P76 results in a severe loss of function whereas H769 appears to play a minor, supporting role in the function of the charged surface of LLP-2.
evidence: Based on functional assay data

claim: Env L771 overlaps Rev L78 but contributes relatively minor constraints at the nucleotide level, as its selection against polar residues permits multiple codons with high fitness in LLP-2.
source: Env L771 also overlaps Rev L78, but contributes relatively minor constraints at the nucleotide level, as its selection against polar residues, rather than for a particular side chain, permits multiple codons with high fitness in LLP-2.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data and analysis of codon constraints

claim: The Env cytoplasmic tail is moderately conserved between HIV-1 clades and the extent of sequence variation is similar in regions that do or do not overlap with Rev.
source: The Env cytoplasmic tail is moderately conserved between HIV-1 clades and the extent of their sequence variation is similar in regions that do or do not overlap with Rev (Steckbeck et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steckbeck et al., 2011

claim: The four distinct HIV-1 lineage groups (M, N, O, P) share similarity with other primate lentiviruses that originated from two different simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) and all have overlapping LLP-2/NES regions.
source: The four distinct HIV-1 lineage groups (M, N, O, P) share similarity with other primate lentiviruses that originated from two different simian immunodeficiency viruses (SIV) and all have overlapping LLP-2/NES regions (Figure 8).
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 8

claim: The hydrophobic Crm1-binding residues of the NES are highly conserved across different HIV-1, HIV-2, and SIVs.
source: The hydrophobic Crm1-binding residues of the NES are highly conserved across different HIV-1, HIV-2, and SIVs (Figure 8) but the NESs can be broadly grouped into two categories: one contains the hydrophobic/proline arrangement observed in HIV-1 and the other contains HIV-2-like characteristics that preserve the spaced hydrophobic contacts but lack consecutive prolines and instead are glutamine-rich.
evidence: Based on sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: LLP-2 sequences in primate lentiviruses fall into three groupings: (1) HIV-1 M, N, and SIVcpzPtt conserve the charge cluster; (2) HIV-1 O, HIV-1 P, SIVgor, and SIVcpzPts have minimal charge; and (3) SIVmac, HIV-2, SIVsmm, and SIVrcm conserve R772 and occasionally D773.
source: LLP-2 is more varied and viruses fall into three groupings: (1) HIV-1 M, N, and SIVcpzPtt conserve the charge cluster dissected in our assays; (2) HIV-1 O, HIV-1 P, SIVgor, and SIVcpzPts have minimal charge; and (3) SIVmac, HIV-2, SIVsmm, and SIVrcm conserve R772 and occasionally D773.
evidence: Based on sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: The high conservation of hydrophobic Crm1 contacts appears to dominate selection for the NES while maintaining sufficient sequence flexibility for LLP-2 to retain its structure.
source: The high conservation of hydrophobic Crm1 contacts appears to dominate selection for the NES while maintaining sufficient sequence flexibility for LLP-2 to retain its structure.
evidence: Based on comparative sequence analysis

claim: The size of the Env cytoplasmic tail varies among different retroviruses.
source: Indeed, the size of the Env cytoplasmic tail varies among different retroviruses (Tedbury and Freed, 2015), and the loss of the tail is commonly observed when SIV is propagated in human cells, suggesting that both host and viral determinants influence the function and variability of this region (Kodama et al., 1989; Shimizu et al., 1992; Shacklett et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tedbury and Freed, 2015; Kodama et al., 1989; Shimizu et al., 1992; Shacklett et al., 2000

claim: Loss of the Env cytoplasmic tail is commonly observed when SIV is propagated in human cells.
source: Indeed, the size of the Env cytoplasmic tail varies among different retroviruses (Tedbury and Freed, 2015), and the loss of the tail is commonly observed when SIV is propagated in human cells, suggesting that both host and viral determinants influence the function and variability of this region (Kodama et al., 1989; Shimizu et al., 1992; Shacklett et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kodama et al., 1989; Shimizu et al., 1992; Shacklett et al., 2000

claim: Residues can functionally segregate even when both overlapping segments are structured.
source: The present study shows that residues can functionally segregate even when both overlapping segments are structured.
evidence: Main finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: Critical residues in both Rev and Env proteins are located on one face of a helix such that they are spaced periodically in alternative reading frames.
source: Interestingly, we observed that critical residues in both proteins are located on one face of a helix such that they are spaced periodically in alternative reading frames (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on structural and functional analysis shown in Figure 7

claim: The wobble bases of functionally critical codons in one reading frame can be chosen to accommodate critical residues in the alternative frame, while the first two codon bases overlap with more mutation-tolerant residues located on a non-binding surface of the overlapped protein.
source: This arrangement is a consequence of the genetic code where the wobble bases of functionally critical codons in one reading frame can be chosen to accommodate critical residues in the alternative frame, while the first two codon bases overlap with more mutation-tolerant residues located on a non-binding surface of the overlapped protein (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on analysis of genetic code constraints and functional data shown in Figure 7

claim: The non-binding face of the Rev NES helix is highly mutable and capable of sampling nearly every amino acid with roughly equal fitness.
source: The non-binding face of the NES helix is highly mutable and capable of sampling nearly every amino acid with roughly equal fitness.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning data

claim: The striking segregation of function observed for Env LLP-2/Rev NES is made possible by the atypical proline-rich NES and partially redundant function of the LLP-2 positive charges.
source: The striking segregation of function we observe for Env LLP-2/Rev NES is made possible by the atypical proline-rich NES and partially redundant function of the LLP-2 positive charges.
evidence: Based on integration of structural and functional data

claim: The manner of functional segregation in HIV-1 is not necessarily the case for similarly overlapped regions in other lentiviruses, which appear to have different functional requirements based on their sequence conservation.
source: This manner of segregation in HIV-1 is not necessarily the case for similarly overlapped regions in other lentiviruses, which appear to have different functional requirements based on their sequence conservation (Figure 8).
evidence: Based on comparative sequence analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: Env D773 is under strong selective pressure although the precise function of this residue is not known.
source: Our results show that Env D773 is under strong selective pressure although the precise function of this residue is not known.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning and functional assay data

claim: The LLP-2 is transiently surface exposed on the cell membrane during infection.
source: The LLP-2 is transiently surface exposed on the cell membrane during infection (Kalia et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2017), and the cytoplasmic tail can modulate the antigenic properties of Env as a whole (Piai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kalia et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2017; Piai et al., 2020

claim: The cytoplasmic tail of Env can modulate the antigenic properties of Env as a whole.
source: The LLP-2 is transiently surface exposed on the cell membrane during infection (Kalia et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2008; Murphy et al., 2017), and the cytoplasmic tail can modulate the antigenic properties of Env as a whole (Piai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piai et al., 2020

claim: Targeting of the LLP-2 surface with combinations of rationally designed immunotherapies may force the virus to mutate in ways that break the segregation between Env and Rev.
source: Targeting of the LLP-2 surface with combinations of rationally designed immunotherapies may force the virus to mutate in ways that break the segregation between Env and Rev.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on the findings

claim: Deep mutational scanning has proven effective at mapping probable mutational escape pathways from immune pressures such as neutralizing antibodies.
source: Deep mutational scanning has proven effective at mapping probable mutational escape pathways from immune pressures such as neutralizing antibodies (Starr et al., 2020; Greaney et al., 2021) and the Env cytoplasmic tail has proven to be a viable target in primate animal models Wang et al., 2020; for HIV-1 the combined knowledge of both functional constraints in the proteins and coding constraints in the genome may allow targeted immune therapies that drastically limit (or prevent altogether) escape mutations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Starr et al., 2020; Greaney et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2020

claim: The Env cytoplasmic tail has proven to be a viable target in primate animal models.
source: Deep mutational scanning has proven effective at mapping probable mutational escape pathways from immune pressures such as neutralizing antibodies (Starr et al., 2020; Greaney et al., 2021) and the Env cytoplasmic tail has proven to be a viable target in primate animal models Wang et al., 2020; for HIV-1 the combined knowledge of both functional constraints in the proteins and coding constraints in the genome may allow targeted immune therapies that drastically limit (or prevent altogether) escape mutations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2020

claim: Immune targeting of overlapped reading frames in in vivo models has been shown to drive predictable synonymous mutations in the alternative, non-targeted frame.
source: Indeed, immune targeting of overlapped reading frames in in vivo models has been shown to drive predictable synonymous mutations in the alternative, non-targeted frame (Hughes et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hughes et al., 2001

claim: Functional segregation occurs in the Rev-Env overlap, with each protein spacing its functional residues in a manner that allows a mutable non-binding face of one helix to encode important functional residues on a charged face in the other helix.
source: We find that functional segregation occurs even in this overlap, with each protein spacing its functional residues in a manner that allows a mutable non-binding face of one helix to encode important functional residues on a charged face in the other helix.
evidence: Main finding of the study based on experimental data

claim: The experiments reveal novel and critical functional residues in Env.
source: Additionally, our experiments reveal novel and critical functional residues in Env and have implications for the therapeutic targeting of HIV-1.
evidence: Based on deep mutational scanning and functional assay data

claim: The NL4-3 rev-in-nef virus has rev moved to the non-essential, single-frame nef locus and the endogenous rev locus is ablated.
source: Briefly, we used the NL4-3 rev-in-nef virus in which rev is moved to the non-essential, single-frame nef locus (Fernandes et al., 2016), and the endogenous rev locus is ablated, thus allowing the endogenous Env LLP-2 region and the rev-in-nef NES region to evolve independently from one another.
evidence: Description of experimental system with citation to Fernandes et al., 2016

claim: Each of the LLP-2 residues in the endogenous env locus was individually randomized, creating 10 Env libraries that each represent 64 alleles (every possible codon).
source: We individually randomized each of the LLP-2 residues in the endogenous env locus, creating 10 Env libraries that each represent 64 alleles (every possible codon).
evidence: Description of experimental method

claim: SupT1 cells were infected at low MOI with each library individually and the change in allele frequencies was measured after approximately six generations of viral spread.
source: Next, we infected SupT1 cells at low MOI (multiplicity of infection) with each library individually and measured the change in allele frequencies after approximately six generations of viral spread (Figure 3A).
evidence: Description of experimental method shown in Figure 3A
